newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK INDUSTRY SAYS FARMERS' BLOCKADE COSTS HEAVY.
newsitem.headline: GREEK INDUSTRY SAYS FARMERS' BLOCKADE COSTS HEAVY.

text.p: A poll of 2,000 industrial firms by Greek industry group SEB on the economic costs of the 20-day farmers blockade of national roads showed that reduced output, and delivery delays endangered permanent market share losses.
Blocked national autoroutes forced companies to lower their output as they were unable to obtain primary inputs and deliver finished products to clients.
The drop in output based on the group of respondents was 6.0 billion drachmas or 2.0 percent of 1995 sales.
"If we assume that this percentage applies industry-wide, the drop in output effectively means a 0.2 percent decrease in 1996 GDP," SEB said in a statement.
Respondents said delays in delivery of goods amounted to 11.7 billion domestically and 8.2 billion abroad, or 2.5 and 1.8 percent of 1995 sales respectively.
"Assuming that the drop in foreign deliveries applies industry-wide, the decrease amounts to over 5.0 percent of Greece's industrial exports," SEB said.
Respondents also said that they had reduced employment time by 14 percent on average during the farmers' blockade.
But most significant was a looming danger of permanent market share loss because of delayed deliveries, the majority, 58 percent, of the respondents felt.

Most concerned were companies based in Macedonia (65%) compared to others in central Greece (51%). Only 10 percent of the respondents said they did not fear any permanent market share loss because of the blockade.
SEB polled 2,000 industrial firms nationwide between December 12-16 and got 240 responses. The response rate was higher in Macedonia (14.3%), Thessaly (12.7%) and central Greece (10.3%).
"It should be noted that a large number of firms responded immediately and this indicates the seriousness of the problem they are faced with," SEB said.
The 240 respondents make up 7.0 percent of Greek industry's 1995 sales which amounted to 461 billion drachmas, SEB said. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
